clue.text: New cars he's wrecked with this cleaner

indicators.note: a wrecked thing is smashed apart, so the letters before it are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone has smashed up some new cars and needs something to clean up with.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the surface: screenwash is what you would use on the cars, so the whole clue reads naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: Screenwash is the fluid squirted onto a car's windscreen to clear dirt, a product for cleaning glass.

clue.text: Neither considered nor armed response on tap here!

definitions.text: Neither considered nor armed response on tap here!

blocks.note: surface reading: a reaction that is thoughtless, and not a police firearms response either
setter's reading: the reflex a doctor gets by tapping just below the kneecap, a leg response, so not an arm one

explanation.surface: A police reaction that was neither thought through nor armed, apparently available on demand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Armed response' suggests police with guns, but the reflex is a kick of the leg, not the arm, and 'on tap' is the doctor's hammer tapping it.
explanation.definitionFit: A knee-jerk reaction is automatic and unthinking, named after the leg reflex triggered by tapping below the kneecap.

clue.text: Countersign a safe deal: a "No tick" offered to DSS persons or affluent characters

annotation.answer: PLEASE DO NOT ASK FOR CREDIT AS A REFUSAL OFTEN OFFENDS

definitions.note: read as a sign displayed on a shop counter

indicators.note: the characters of the preceding phrase are its letters, which are to be taken and set out afresh

blocks.clueFragment: a safe deal: a "No tick" offered to DSS persons or affluent
blocks.note: every letter of the phrase, punctuation dropped

explanation.surface: A shop insists on cash, refusing credit (on tick) whether customers are on benefits or rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Countersign' looks like the verb for adding a second signature; here it is a sign on a counter. 'On tick' is British slang for on credit, and the DSS was the benefits department.
explanation.definitionFit: This notice is the classic jokey card propped beside a shop till, so it is literally a sign for a counter.

indicators.note: to reverse is to go backwards, so the short word before it is read back to front

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
taken as written

explanation.surface: Driving instructions: how to reverse the car is to steer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' reads as a verb about driving, but it is the noun, a young bullock. STOT is a Scots and northern English word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A stot is a bullock or young castrated ox, which is exactly what a steer is in cattle farming.

indicators.note: something disputed is argued over and pulled about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A contested title deed concerns some islands, the kind of quarrel that sovereignty over island groups often provokes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dodecanese are a group of Greek islands in the south-eastern Aegean, Rhodes the largest of them.

clue.text: Dante, or his sister, consuming congealed Swiss potatoes

indicators.note: something consuming another takes it inside, so the word for congealed goes within the dish

blocks.note: rösti is the Swiss fried grated-potato cake
jelly that has congealed has set

explanation.surface: Someone, possibly a famous Italian, is tucking into a cold, congealed plate of Swiss potatoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dante' suggests the Italian poet, but this is Dante Gabriel Rossetti, the Pre-Raphaelite painter, whose sister was the poet Christina.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante Gabriel Rossetti and his sister Christina Rossetti share the surname, so either one is named by it.

clue.text: Not stressed, but needing a pick-me-up

blocks.note: taken as written
a tonic is a restorative drink or medicine

explanation.surface: Someone is relaxed and not stressed, yet still in need of something to perk them up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not stressed' sounds like calm, but it is the phonetic term for an unaccented syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: In phonetics an atonic syllable or word carries no accent, so it is unstressed in speech.

clue.text: Joan temporised a little before the stake

indicators.note: only a little of the words is wanted, a short run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters straddling the end of the name and the start of the verb

explanation.surface: Joan stalled for a while before something was at stake, perhaps a gambler hesitating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' joins the parts and nods at the word itself, which is Latin for before.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the ante is the stake each player puts into the pot before the cards are dealt.

blocks.note: surface reading: a man from Venice, or a Venetian blind
setter's reading: cuts are canals, and his life's work was paintings of the waterways of his home city

explanation.surface: A Venetian edits or trims down his own body of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts' looks like a verb, but a cut is a canal, so the painter's oeuvre is Venetian canal views.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century painter famed for detailed views of Venice and its Grand Canal fits a man whose work is waterways.

clue.text: Such a fowl as the owl? Nonsense!

definitions.text: Such a fowl as the owl? Nonsense!

blocks.clueFragment: Such a fowl as the owl?
blocks.note: surface reading: an owl is hardly a fowl, a scornful question
setter's reading: Edward Lear's nonsense verse, where the Pussy-cat calls the Owl a fowl with this adjective

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea that an owl counts as a fowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nonsense!' reads as an exclamation of disbelief, but points to Lear's Book of Nonsense; in The Owl and the Pussy-cat she sings to him of his charm.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lear's poem the Pussy-cat addresses the Owl as a graceful, stylish fowl, the very adjective required here.

clue.text: The nature of de Gaulle's driving force

blocks.note: first meaning: the intrinsic core of something
second meaning: the French word for petrol, what powers a Frenchman's car

explanation.surface: An enquiry into what really drove Charles de Gaulle as a leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving force' sounds like ambition, but de Gaulle signals French, and the force is the fuel driving a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the fundamental nature of a thing, and in French it is the ordinary word for petrol fuel.

clue.text: Relative that is found in Newchurch

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so the abbreviation goes within the other letters

blocks.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is; 'that' read with the following 'is'
split as New, abbreviated N, and church, the Church of England abbreviated CE

explanation.surface: A family member turns up living in a village called Newchurch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newchurch' looks like one place name; split it into New and church. 'That is' gives IE, its 'is' doing double duty with 'found in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is a family member, the daughter of one's brother or sister, so she counts as a relative.

blocks.note: first meaning: sensible and workable, as in sound advice
second meaning: Macavity is one of T. S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of ... Cats

explanation.surface: Someone does an impression of the noises made by Macavity the mystery cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound like' suggests a noise or a homophone, but Sound is a separate adjective; Eliot's cats, Macavity among them, are titled this way.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means sensible and workable, and Eliot's book called its cats by the same word.

clue.text: Body of demonstrators against joining Labour?

definitions.text: Body of demonstrators against joining Labour?

blocks.clueFragment: Body of demonstrators against joining Labour
blocks.note: surface reading: protesters opposed to signing up with the Labour Party
setter's reading: strikers outside a workplace who oppose anyone going in to work, labour in the lower-case sense

explanation.surface: A protest group campaigns against people becoming Labour Party members.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L points to the political party; read it as labour, work, and the demonstrators are strikers urging others not to work.
explanation.definitionFit: A picket line is the row of striking workers outside a workplace trying to dissuade others from entering to work.

definitions.note: loosely; the leaf insect is a cousin of the stick insect, not a true cockroach

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters before it are scattered and rebuilt

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A cockroach found in a café has been allowed to escape.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: leaf insects are related to stick insects, though older classifications lumped them with cockroaches.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf insect is a large flat insect camouflaged like foliage, here treated broadly as a cockroach-like creature.

clue.text: How co-stars play or work both ways on location

blocks.note: OP, short for opus, a work, written forwards and then backwards
a site is a location

explanation.surface: A question about how two co-stars act together, or perform when filming on location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On location' reads as film jargon; here it simply puts SITE last.
explanation.definitionFit: Co-stars play opposite each other, each acting as the other's counterpart in the leading roles.

blocks.note: AB is an able seaman, so sailors are ABS
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sailors have fallen overboard, the drink being slang for the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the drink' means in the sea, so the drink looks like water; it is the liquor, and the phrase before it spells it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Absinthe is a strong green anise-flavoured spirit made with wormwood, so it is an alcoholic drink.

indicators.note: heard means we go by how the words sound when spoken, not how they are spelt

blocks.note: to hire a piece of equipment is to pay for its use

explanation.surface: A short instruction about paying for something, overheard, then a switch.
explanation.walkthrough: A switch is a tress of false hair, not a light switch. The sound match is loose, depending on a clipped pronunciation of hire.
explanation.definitionFit: A switch is a length of detached hair added to a hairstyle, which is a kind of false hair addition.

clue.text: Chicken Newton preserved in ... in fat

indicators.note: something preserved in fat is sealed inside it, so the unit letter sits within the word

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

explanation.surface: A recipe: chicken with something called Newton preserved in fat, like a confit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' looks like the bird in a recipe; it is a youngster, as in no spring chicken. The ellipsis and repeated in carry the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken can mean a young person or child, and an infant is a baby or very young child.

indicators.note: a replacement swaps things around, so the letters of the opening words are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A substitute announces he is taking over and tells the other man to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: IMSHI is old British Army slang, picked up in Egypt from Arabic, for go away.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a soldiers' slang command meaning go away, the same sense as telling someone to clear off.

blocks.note: surface reading: creative inspiration that never runs dry
setter's reading: inspiration as drawing breath in, a movement inwards, the opposite of a tide going out

explanation.surface: An artist's inspiration that never fades away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiration' suggests creative ideas, but it literally means breathing in, a movement inwards like a tide coming in rather than going out.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspiration in the literal sense is an intake, a movement inwards, and what does not ebb is a flood coming in.

clue.text: John, Free Democrat hero of Exmoor

blocks.note: to free of something is to rid of it
D is the abbreviation for Democrat

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat named John is lauded as Exmoor's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: John Ridd is the hero of R. D. Blackmore's novel Lorna Doone, set on Exmoor, moorland in south-west England. 'Free Democrat' looks like a party name.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ridd is the farmer narrator and hero of Lorna Doone, whose story is set on the Exmoor moors.

indicators.note: the long word sheds some of its letters at each end, leaving a run from its middle

blocks.note: the run of letters in the middle of the name of the statue

explanation.surface: The famous discus-thrower statue might do with slimming down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Discobolus is the classical statue of a discus thrower. An obol was an ancient Greek coin and also a small unit of weight.
explanation.definitionFit: The obol was a small ancient Greek weight, about a sixth of a drachm, later also an apothecaries' unit.

clue.text: Like Scott's revival of The Goon Show, I see!

indicators.note: to show something is to put it on display in a fresh arrangement, so the letters are laid out anew

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the letter C is pronounced see

explanation.surface: Someone notices that The Goon Show, the classic BBC radio comedy, is being revived.
explanation.walkthrough: The Goon Show was a 1950s BBC radio comedy. Sir George Gilbert Scott led the Victorian Gothic revival, designing St Pancras station.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gilbert Scott's buildings revived medieval Gothic forms, which is precisely the nineteenth-century Gothic Revival style.
